title: Part V — LEADERSHIP: Roles, Spans and Layers

know: The part answers four questions in order, one per chapter: Which executive roles does a product and tech organization need, and who should report to whom?; How should product, engineering and design share decisions at each level?; Given the team sizes of chapter 8, how many people should a manager have, how many layers follow, and what does each layer cost?; What do senior technical leaders own that managers do not?
can_do: Pick the chapter of this part that answers the question in front of them.

audience.who: Executives and individual contributors in product and tech who have read Parts I to IV and are about to start Part V, or who arrive with one question about leadership roles, managers or senior technical roles and want the chapter that answers it.
already_knows: What a CTO, a CPO, a VP Engineering, an engineering manager and a staff engineer are, as job titles.

Parts I to IV in outline: judgment as one of the three capacities that run out, decision rights as one of the four levers, team size (chapter 8), the product model in which leaders own problems and teams own solutions, and the engineering model of policies, governance and platforms.
does_not_know: Joining decisions as the work that defines a leader; defined here.
Executive configurations (peers, one combined executive, CTO with VP Engineering) (chapter 18); named and glossed here.
The triad of product, engineering and design with one accountable role per risk (chapter 19); glossed here.
Span, layer and manager of managers (chapter 20); glossed here.
Staff-plus and the technical leadership track (chapter 21); glossed here.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of this page alone can name the four chapters' subjects in reading order.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only this page: what will each of the next four chapters tell you, in order?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Executive Roles and Reporting Lines; The Product–Engineering–Design Triad; Spans, Layers and Managers of Managers; Staff-Plus and Architects.

thesis.question: Who leads a product and tech organization, how are leaders arranged, and what is each layer for?
thesis.claim: Leadership structure is derived, not chosen from a template: executive roles follow from which decisions must be joined at the top, the product–engineering–design triad repeats at every level where those decisions recur, spans and layers follow from team size, each layer existing to join decisions that the units below it cannot join themselves, and a technical leadership track carries the decisions that management structure cannot.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that leadership structure is a matter of the people available — give strong leaders scope and titles that keep them — and the template view that every company of a given size should have the same roles.
thesis.so_what: A leader can explain each role and layer by the decisions it joins, and can remove or decline one that joins none.
thesis.how_why: A leader's distinctive work is joining decisions that would otherwise be made separately: product with engineering, one group with another, this quarter with next year. Where decisions need joining is set by the architecture of Parts II to IV, so the leadership structure follows from it; and judgment, the capacity leaders hold, is scarce, so each layer must earn the delay it adds.

supporting_claims.claim: Executive roles and reporting lines follow from which decisions must be joined at the top, and each common configuration trades one kind of joining for another.

Product, engineering and design decide together at every level where their decisions recur, with each accountable for one risk, and the triad fails when one of the three becomes order-giver, veto or decoration.
Spans and layers are derived from team size, and each layer costs delay and distance from information that must be justified by decisions only it can join.
A technical leadership track holds the cross-team technical decisions that the management line is not placed to make, and it works when its accountability is explicit.

role.contribution: Performs the part's opening: states the part thesis and the reading order.

additional_patterns.applies_to: four-places and the chapter list in the closing: the executive level, then the triad at every level, then spans and layers between the top and the teams, then the technical track across teams

flow.rationale: The page opens on two leaders whose drawings of the same organization disagree, and on the question of what each role is for. The first section says what a leader's distinctive work is, joining decisions, why that makes the structure something to derive, and what limits it; the second gives the four places where decisions are joined and says why they are read from the top down; the chapter list closes the page. The work of joining stands before the four places because each place is justified by decisions that need joining there; put the places first and executive roles, triads, layers and a technical track arrive as a template, which is the view the part disputes. The list comes last because a reader can choose a chapter only after seeing what each one derives.

hook.content: In 2025, when Corvane appointed its first CPO, the CTO and the CPO each drew the organization they needed, and the two drawings disagreed about who led eleven of the teams.

bridge.from_reader_world: The reader's experience of a leadership structure shaped by who was available and who had to be kept.
bridge.to_topic: The question that experience raises and that the usual answers (fit the chart to the people, or copy the roles of a company the same size) skip: what each role is for.

thesis_statement.text: Part V argues that leadership structure is derived, not chosen from a template: executive roles follow from which decisions must be joined at the top, the product, engineering and design triad repeats at every level where those decisions recur, spans and layers follow from team size, and a technical leadership track carries the decisions that the management structure cannot.

promises.promise: What a leader's distinctive work is, and why it makes the structure something to derive.

The four places where decisions are joined and why they are read from the top down; four chapters answer four questions in order: which executive roles and who reports to whom, how product, engineering and design decide together, how many people a manager leads and how many layers follow, and what senior technical leaders own.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2025, when Priya Nambiar became Corvane's first CPO, she and the CTO, Tomas Rell, each drew the organization they needed, and the two drawings disagreed about who led eleven of the teams.

evidence.what: Corvane (fictional): in 2025, as the company grew from 180 people toward 500, Priya Nambiar was appointed its first CPO; she and Tomas Rell, co-founder and CTO, each drew the organization they needed; the drawings disagreed about who led eleven of the teams.
evidence.source: _research/scenario-ledger.md (Part V opening and its correction line)
evidence.shows: Two reasonable drawings of one organization that cannot both be right, with no stated ground for choosing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A leadership structure is usually settled by the people available and the people who must be kept, or copied from a template for a company of that size, and the question both skip is what each role is for; without an answer two drawings can only be compared by who drew them.

evidence.what: Each drawing can be defended by the strengths of the people on it; neither says what a leader of those teams would decide that nobody else can, so there is nothing to test either drawing against.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json, part-5 opening bridge and disputed_by
evidence.shows: Why neither the people view nor the template view settles a disagreement like Corvane's.

transition_in.introduces: The reader's own version of a structure shaped by people, the two usual views, and the question that both skip.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Part V argues that leadership structure is derived from the decisions that must be joined and is not chosen from a template, and it makes the argument in four chapters that answer four questions in order.

transition_in.carries_over: The question of what each role is for.
transition_in.introduces: The part's claim, which answers it, and the four questions its chapters take in turn.

sections.heading: What a Leader Is For
sections.controlling_idea: A leader's distinctive work is joining decisions that would otherwise be made separately; where decisions need joining is set by the architecture of Parts II to IV, so the leadership structure follows from it, and because judgment is scarce and every layer adds delay, each role and layer must earn its place by the decisions it joins.

advances_thesis.how: States the reasoning from which the part derives every role and layer.

transition_in.carries_over: The part's claim as stated in the lead.
transition_in.introduces: The reasoning that produces it: what a leader does that nobody else is placed to do.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A leader's distinctive work is joining decisions that would otherwise be made separately (product with engineering, one group with another, this quarter with next year); where that joining is needed is set by the teams, product model and engineering model of Parts II to IV, so the leadership structure can be derived from them.

evidence.what: To join two decisions is to make them in one place, so that each takes account of the other. A leader's distinctive work is joining decisions that would otherwise be made separately: product with engineering, one group with another, this quarter with next year. Where decisions need joining is set by the architecture of Parts II to IV.
evidence.shows: Why the structure of leadership is a consequence of the structure of teams and operating models, and not a separate choice.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Joining has a cost: judgment, the capacity leaders hold, is scarce and every layer adds delay and distance from information, so each role and layer must earn its place; the test corresponds to the two lenses through which the book looks at organizations, named here before they are used: saying where a decision is joined is system design, and judging a role or layer by what it does for the teams below it is product thinking.

evidence.what: Judgment, deciding with the relevant information at hand (chapter 1), is scarce; each layer adds a step of delay and of distance from the information, so each layer must earn the delay it adds by joining decisions the units below it cannot join themselves.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json, part-5 how_why and P5-3; chapter 1's definition of judgment
evidence.shows: The limit that keeps 'leaders join decisions' from justifying any number of leaders.

transition_in.carries_over: Joining decisions as the work that justifies a leader.
transition_in.introduces: What the joining costs, and the test each role and layer has to pass.

sections.heading: Four Places Where Decisions Are Joined
sections.controlling_idea: Decisions are joined in four places (at the top, across the three functions at every level, down the management line, and across teams on technical questions), and the part reads them from the top down because each is defined by the one before.

advances_thesis.how: One list item per supporting claim, then the order.

flow.rationale: The executive level comes first because its configuration decides where product and engineering meet; the triad then shows the same meeting at every level below; spans and layers say how many levels there are between the top and the teams; the technical track comes last because it is defined by what that management structure leaves unowned. The paragraph on the order closes the section because the dependency can be stated only once all four places have been met; start with spans and the layers are counted before anyone knows what the top layer is.

transition_in.carries_over: Joining decisions, and the test each role and layer must pass.
transition_in.introduces: The four places where the part applies that test, one per chapter.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Decisions are joined in four places: at the top, where executive roles and reporting lines follow from which decisions must be joined there; across functions, where product, engineering and design decide together as a triad at every level, each accountable for one risk; down the line, where spans and layers follow from team size and each layer must join decisions the units below it cannot; and across teams, where a technical leadership track holds the technical decisions the management line is not placed to make.

advances_thesis.how: Names the four places with their terms glossed, one per supporting claim.

evidence.what: The rule of thumb that a manager of managers leads about four to six managers (Will Larson, An Elegant Puzzle, 2019), presented as Larson's rule of thumb; the rest is the part's own claims.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json entries of chapters 18 to 21; PLAN.md anchors
evidence.shows: That spans are a named source's rule of thumb, which chapter 20 presents and tests.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The four places are read from the top down, the executive level first because its configuration decides where product and engineering meet, the triad next because it is the same meeting repeated below, spans and layers third because they say how many levels there are, and the technical track last because it is defined by what the management line leaves unowned; every chapter carries both lenses, and the part draws on two earlier ones: spans start from the team sizes of Part II, and the technical track holds the roles on which the governance of Part IV already relied.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the four supporting claims as steps that each depend on the one before.

evidence.what: The executive configuration decides where product and engineering meet; the triad is that meeting at every level; spans and layers give the structure between the top and the teams, from the team sizes of chapter 8; the technical track is defined by what that structure leaves unowned; the governance of chapter 14 relies on its roles, so the dependency on Part IV runs the same way as in p04 (Part IV is the input). Starting with spans would count layers before knowing what the top layer is.
evidence.source: journal-spec.json, part-5 flow rationale and the entries of chapters 20 and 21
evidence.shows: Why the chapters are read in this order.

transition_in.introduces: The order in which each depends on the one before, and where the book's two lenses and the earlier parts appear in them.

conclusion.heading: Chapters in this part
conclusion.synthesis: Read in order, the four chapters build a leadership structure from the top down and then across: the roles at the top, the three functions deciding together at each level, the number of levels and managers, and the technical roles that cross them.
conclusion.so_what: A leader can explain each role and layer by the decisions it joins, and can remove or decline one that joins none.

callback.to: The two drawings of Corvane's organization from the opening (p01).
callback.how: The closing reads the drawings against the lead's question: the CTO and the CPO argued about who should lead the eleven teams and nobody had asked what each role was for, which is why both drawings could be defended and neither could be shown to be right.

takeaway.content: Read the chapters in order; with one question about leadership structure in hand, open the chapter that answers it.

transition_in.introduces: The chapters one by one, each with the question it answers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Each of the four chapters answers one question, in this order: which executive roles are needed and who reports to whom, how product, engineering and design share decisions at each level, how many people a manager should have and how many layers follow, and what senior technical leaders own that managers do not.

The four chapters build a leadership structure from the top down and then across; at Corvane the two leaders argued about who should lead the eleven teams and nobody had asked what each role was for; a leader who has the four answers can explain each role and layer by the decisions it joins and can remove or decline one that joins none, and the first chapter starts at the executive level, where the first joining is made or missed.

decision_log.decision: The post entry in the journal spec has a question and no thesis. A part introduction performs the part's opening, so this spec uses the part's thesis and its four supporting claims P5-1 to P5-4 unchanged; they are the part's, not the page's own. rejected: A separate reading-order section after the list.

decision_log.decision: The four chapters of Part V are not written yet, so the page describes them from their journal-spec entries only and names no worked example of theirs.

decision_log.decision: Flow rubric (one fresh reader, order of ideas only): sound with notes. Taken: p05 introduces the two lenses as the book's before using them; p07 states the tie to Part IV in the same direction as p04 (Part IV is an input: its governance relies on the roles the technical track holds), where the first wording read as a hand-off to Part IV.
rejected: Merging the chapter list into the list of the four places: the page format ends with 'Chapters in this part', and AC-1 and the brief require the list of links with their questions.

decision_log.decision: Accepted in auto mode by the author's standing instruction of 2026-11-19; not individually reviewed.
